steps.explanationAfterStep: The pair flows from the α-carbon through the imine into the ring and ends on the ring nitrogen: the protonated pyridine is the electron sink, like the C=O of an enolate. The enzyme holds the α-C–H bond perpendicular to the ring plane so that it overlaps with the π system (Dunathan's proposal).

The same lysine puts the proton on the other end of the conjugated system. The net result is that the C=N has moved: an aldimine (C=N on the PLP side) has become a ketimine (C=N on the amino acid side). This is the heart of transamination. The proton is delivered to one face only; the app does not check stereochemistry yet.
Hydrolysis starts, exactly as for any iminium ion.
The nitrogen is protonated so that it can leave as a neutral amine.

Pyruvate is released; the nitrogen of alanine stays behind on the cofactor as pyridoxamine (PMP). In the second half of the cycle the same steps run backwards with 2-oxoglutarate, which leaves as glutamate and gives back PLP.

title: PLP: transamination
subtitle: Pyridoxal phosphate moves an amino group from alanine to the cofactor
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 42
Berg, Tymoczko, Gatto and Stryer, Biochemistry (W. H. Freeman), chapter 23: amino acid degradation (pyridoxal phosphate, transamination)

ketimine.caption: the ketimine: the C=N has moved to the former amino acid carbon
hintTiers: Hydrolysis of an iminium ion is imine formation run backwards. Water is the nucleophile; lysine is the base.
The lysine nitrogen takes the drawn hydrogen of water, that O–H pair becomes the new bond from oxygen to the C=N⁺ carbon, and the C=N⁺ π pair goes onto nitrogen. Three arrows.
Lysine lone pair → new bond to the drawn hydrogen of water; that O–H bond → new bond from the water oxygen to the C=N⁺ carbon; C=N⁺ π bond → a lone pair on the imine nitrogen.
ketimine.learnerPrompt: Hydrolyse the ketimine: water attacks the C=N⁺ carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking that proton off again goes back to the quinonoid intermediate. Hydrolyse the ketimine.
That carbon is now a CH₂, with no C=N. Water attacks the C=N⁺ carbon, the former α-carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right attack, but the water oxygen would be left positive. Let lysine take its proton at the same time.

quinonoid.caption: the quinonoid intermediate + protonated lysine
hintTiers: The quinonoid intermediate is nucleophilic at both ends of the conjugated system. Protonation at the α-carbon would just give back the aldimine. Push from the ring nitrogen instead.

The ring nitrogen lone pair re-forms C=N⁺ in the ring, a ring C=C moves along, the exocyclic C=C π pair takes the drawn hydrogen of the lysine ammonium ion, and that N–H pair stays on the lysine nitrogen. Four arrows.

Ring nitrogen lone pair → π bond to the next ring carbon; that ring C=C π bond → π bond to the ring carbon bearing the side chain; the exocyclic C=C π bond → new bond from the outer carbon to the drawn hydrogen of the lysine ammonium ion; that N–H bond → a lone pair on the lysine nitrogen.
quinonoid.learnerPrompt: Lysine puts the proton back, this time on the carbon next to the ring.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Putting the proton back on the α-carbon reverses the last step (that is what amino acid racemases do). Put it on the carbon next to the ring.
The quinonoid intermediate is electron-rich: water has nothing to attack yet.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right proton, right carbon, but the ring would be left with a cation. Push the ring nitrogen lone pair back into the ring.

reactants.caption: the external aldimine: alanine bound to PLP (a model: the CH₂OPO₃²⁻ side chain drawn as CH₃) + lysine (methylamine) + water
hintTiers: PLP is an electron sink. The protonated imine and the pyridinium ring together can take the C–H pair all the way to the ring nitrogen.

The lysine nitrogen takes the drawn α-hydrogen; that C–H pair forms C=N with the imine nitrogen; the imine C=N⁺ π pair moves to the bond to the ring; a ring C=C moves along; and the C=N⁺ π pair of the ring goes onto the ring nitrogen. Five arrows.

Lysine lone pair → new bond to the α-hydrogen; that C–H bond → π bond from the α-carbon to the imine nitrogen; the imine C=N π bond → π bond from the imine carbon to the ring carbon; that ring carbon's C=C π bond → π bond to the next ring carbon along; the ring C=N⁺ π bond → a lone pair on the ring nitrogen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Lysine removes the α-hydrogen of the amino acid. Where do the electrons go?

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Loss of CO₂ is what PLP decarboxylases do (making GABA or dopamine, for example). An aminotransferase holds the α-C–H bond in line with the π system instead, so the proton is the group that leaves.
Water adding to the aldimine would just hydrolyse it back to PLP and alanine. First remove the α-hydrogen.
Lysine adding to the aldimine carbon is how the amino acid was bound (transaldimination), run backwards. Here lysine is the base.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right so far, but stopping at the imine carbon leaves a carbanion. PLP can do better: push the pair on into the ring, all the way to the ring nitrogen.

carbinolamine.caption: the carbinolamine + protonated lysine
hintTiers: The amine must leave as a neutral molecule. Which acid is there?
The nitrogen lone pair takes the drawn hydrogen of the lysine ammonium ion, and that N–H pair stays on the lysine nitrogen. Two arrows.
Carbinolamine nitrogen lone pair → new bond to the drawn hydrogen of the lysine ammonium ion; that N–H bond → a lone pair on the lysine nitrogen.
carbinolamine.learnerPrompt: Make the nitrogen into a leaving group.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Losing the OH again goes back to the ketimine. Protonate the nitrogen.
An amide anion (R–NH⁻) is a terrible leaving group. Protonate the nitrogen first.

carbinolammonium.caption: the protonated carbinolamine + lysine
hintTiers: Lysine takes the O–H proton, and that pair forms the C=O as the neutral amine leaves.
The lysine nitrogen takes the drawn O–H hydrogen, that O–H pair forms the C=O π bond, and the C–N bond breaks onto nitrogen. Three arrows.
Lysine lone pair → new bond to the drawn O–H hydrogen; that O–H bond → C=O π bond; the C–N bond → a lone pair on the nitrogen of the pyridoxamine side.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking the N–H proton back undoes the last step. Use the OH.
Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, and the protonated amine is ready to go.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right bond to break, but the carbon would be left as a cation. Use the OH oxygen's electrons to form C=O, with lysine taking its proton.

mechanismSummary: Aminotransferases use pyridoxal phosphate (PLP). The amino acid (alanine) is bound to PLP as a protonated imine, the external aldimine. A lysine removes the α-hydrogen, and the pair flows through the imine into the pyridinium ring, which acts as an electron sink: the quinonoid intermediate. The lysine puts the proton back on the carbon next to the ring, so the C=N has moved to the amino acid side (a ketimine). Hydrolysis releases pyruvate and leaves pyridoxamine (PMP), which passes the amino group on to 2-oxoglutarate in the second half of the cycle. Models: methylamine for lysine; in PLP the ring's CH₂OPO₃²⁻ side chain takes no part and is drawn as CH₃, and the ring OH (an O⁻ hydrogen-bonded to the imine N–H in the enzyme) is drawn neutral.
